cells.tense: The carrying is steady enough right now that feeling can come in, and you're letting it.
cells.ask: Tell one person, in plain words, what you're carrying today, and stop there, without handing it over. You get back a minute that doesn't have to be earned.
cells.core:
When things are steady, you take the weight that lands on you without gripping shut. You carry the day and stay reachable in it. Someone says something hard and you're still there for the next thing they say, and carrying and feeling aren't two separate jobs.

Right now there's room in you for what's arriving, and you're not deciding anything about it yet. You can tell the load is heavy without closing around it. The way back is the only way back there is: say what you're carrying out loud, once, to the person in front of you today, and leave it unhandled. That's how the opening stays open.
cells.sheetLine: You can carry it and still feel it coming in.
cells.verb: opening before there is anything to hold
cells.place: in the part of you that keeps carrying it after it stops making sense

cells.tense: You're already bracing for a version of this that hasn't happened yet, and your hands are full with it.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you're holding for tomorrow and set it down on paper tonight, a line only, not a plan. You get to feel your own footing on today's ground again.
cells.core:
On a good day here, you carry what's actually in front of you. You finish one load and put it down, then pick up the next thing the day asks for. Each load is real and current, and that's what keeps you steady.

The trouble now is that you're holding what hasn't arrived. You're rehearsing how to survive it before it's yours, and today can't get through because your arms are full of a day that hasn't come. Holding it ahead of time feels like being ready. What it costs is the one load that's actually here, the one you could put down tonight if you wrote it out.
cells.sheetLine: You're carrying tomorrow, so today can't land.
cells.verb: opening before there is anything to hold
cells.place: in the part of you that keeps carrying it after it stops making sense

cells.tense: Something got heavy and you kept carrying it past the point where you could feel it.
cells.ask: Set one object in front of you, a mug or a key, anything in reach, and look at it for a full minute without doing anything else. You get proof that what's in front of you still reaches you.
cells.core:
At your best, you can stand in something hard and stay open to the person next to you. You hold what needs holding and you're in the room while you do it, and one doesn't cancel the other.

What's run quiet is the receiving side. You're still carrying, but lifting and setting down happen on their own, and now you brace on reflex even for things you could take in. Nothing in you is gone. Letting things in has just gone behind the load. Coming back goes through something fresh, not through feeling more. The minute with the mug puts you back in touch with what's right there.
cells.sheetLine: You kept carrying past the point where you could feel the load.

cells.tense: You're already taking things in, and the credit for it landed somewhere else.
cells.ask: Name one small thing today that got into you, a sound or a line or a face, and say 'that one was mine' about it, once, out loud if you're alone. Smallness is the proof; you're not claiming anything large.
cells.core:
On a good day, you take in what reaches you. A song, a sentence, someone's mood across the room: it lands and you let it be yours, and you don't have to do anything with it. That's the open part of you working.

Right now it works and you don't claim it. You describe it as being practical. You mention what the day was like as though the day had said it, not you, and the taking-in keeps happening without you standing behind it. The accuracy is already there. Saying one small thing out loud is how the credit comes back to the person it belongs to.
cells.sheetLine: You're already taking it in. You're just calling it the day's.
